q1: `<!DOCTYPE html>` must be the first line of the file — it puts the browser into standards mode before anything else is parsed.
q2: The doctype's job is to trigger standards mode rendering; without it, older browsers can fall back to quirks mode and render inconsistently.
q3: The `lang` attribute on `<html>` declares the page's language, e.g. `lang="en"`.
q4: `<head>` holds metadata like `title`, `meta charset`, and stylesheet `link` tags — visible content like body text and images belongs in `<body>`.
q5: A document should have exactly one `<body>` element, holding all of the visible content.
q6: `UTF-8` is the standard character encoding declared via `<meta charset="UTF-8">`.
q7: Visible content like `<h1>` doesn't belong inside `<head>` — almost nothing in `<head>` renders on the page, so it should move into `<body>`.
q8: Missing `lang` can cause screen readers to mispronounce text, confuse translation tools, and hurt how search engines target the page by language — but it does not stop the page from rendering.
q9: The correct order is `<!DOCTYPE html>`, then `<html>`, then `<head>`, then `<body>` — the doctype comes first, followed by the root element, then head, then body inside it.
q10: Browsers are lenient with invalid structure like duplicate `<body>` tags — they typically try to recover and merge the content rather than failing, which hides the underlying mistake.
